issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent physical bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on anger, distrust, hypervigilance, and media avoidance after police violence but contains no corroborating threat or memory content about ongoing somatic injury, pain, disability, or bodily fragility. It stands out as a different trauma consequence than the remainder of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling used for excitement/distracting is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The dominant formulation is Threat ↔ Negative Appraisals with trauma-memory-linked fear/anger and avoidance of feelings/media. Gambling for excitement does not clearly address the specific threat, memory, or appraisal pattern represented elsewhere, making it the least coherent maladaptive strategy in this set.

vignette: Amir's life had been forever altered on a sweltering summer evening three years ago. He was walking home from work when he witnessed a group of police officers brutally beating an unarmed teenager. The images seared into his mind like the taste of sweat and smoke that still lingered on his tongue to this day. As he recalled the event, Amir felt an intense rage course through his veins, as if his body was reliving the horror all over again. Since then, Amir had become increasingly withdrawn. He avoided social gatherings, stopped watching TV or reading about similar events, and even changed his daily routine to steer clear of any potential triggers. His reasoning was simple: he couldn't trust others, not after what he saw that day. The world seemed like a treacherous place, where violence could erupt at any moment. Amir's strategy for coping with these fears was to numb himself, avoiding anything that might stir up emotions – positive or negative. As a social media manager, Amir spent most of his days staring at screens, but even this familiar environment felt threatening now. He would constantly scan the room for potential escape routes, mentally mapping out how he could flee if needed. The feeling of being on edge had become so ingrained that Amir couldn't relax, not even in the comfort of his own home with his wife by his side. The memories of that fateful evening still haunted him. When they surfaced, Amir would push them away before he could fully recall the details – a coping mechanism that left him feeling like he was drowning in fragmented images and emotions. His mind was consumed by thoughts of betrayal and distrust; how could people sworn to protect others commit such atrocities? The more he struggled with these questions, the more Amir became convinced that people were not what they seemed. As time went on, Amir's fears only intensified. He started to believe that his actions – or rather, inactions – during the event had violated his own values as a human being. If only he had intervened, maybe things would have turned out differently. The weight of this guilt was crushing him, making it harder for him to connect with others or find meaning in his daily life. The world indeed felt like a perilous place, and Amir's constant threat monitoring had become second nature. His hypervigilance led him to avoid social interactions altogether – if he couldn't trust others, why bother? This avoidance only served to strengthen his negative appraisals, reinforcing the notion that people were untrustworthy. One day, as Amir was working from home, a loud noise outside startled him. He leapt out of his chair, heart racing, and frantically scanned the room for an escape route. It dawned on him then – he couldn't go on living like this. The memories, the fears, the constant hypervigilance – it was all taking a toll on his relationships, his work, and most importantly, his own sense of self. It was this realization that finally brought Amir to seek help. He hoped that by confronting his demons head-on, he could learn to trust again – not just others, but himself.
